items.headline: Where will AI actually move the needle in drug discovery?
items.preview: AI's role in drug discovery is evolving, focusing on biological hypotheses rather than just compound optimization.
items.article:
Artificial intelligence is now a part of everyday language in drug discovery. New companies launch every week with AI at the core, large pharma partnerships are announced monthly, and capital has flowed into some major players at a scale the sector has never seen before.
Why this matters: Improving clinical outcomes is the key goal we are all working towards. However, much of the attention in AI in drug discovery is taken up with compound optimisation rather than biological discovery. The ambition to build a computational 'virtual cell' model capable of predicting how any cell responds to any perturbation could profoundly impact target identification and therapeutic effects.
The critical questions relevant for near-term strategy are one of translation and one of timeline. To move the clinical needle, even exceptionally data-rich models must generate targets and hypotheses that hold up through a chain of translation. The opportunity now is not to model everything everywhere all at once, but to extract high-resolution insights from the right questions and data and convert these into hypotheses worth testing in the clinic.

items.headline: Optoelectronic tweezers may revolutionize single-cell research
items.preview: Optoelectronic tweezers (OETs) are transforming single-cell manipulation with unprecedented precision.
items.article:
Optoelectronic tweezers, or OETs, have evolved from a niche optical manipulation trick into a versatile platform capable of catching, moving, sorting, and interrogating single cells. OETs exploit beams of light projected onto a semiconductor chip to sculpt electric fields that manipulate cells without physical contact.
Why this matters: The adaptability of OET technology allows for high-throughput screening and sorting of cells, integrating with other single-cell technologies for enhanced analysis. This innovation could lead to significant advancements in fields like antibody discovery and cell line development, compressing timelines and improving efficiency in research and clinical applications.

items.headline: The hidden innovation system behind drug repurposing
items.preview: A new model reveals how hospitals and universities drive drug repurposing despite commercial pressures.
items.article:
Pharmaceutical innovation often follows a familiar model, but a recent paper argues that drug repurposing operates under a different system. Hospitals and universities continue to conduct late-stage trials on existing medicines even after patent protections fade, driven by scientific reputation and patient need.
Why this matters: This parallel innovation system highlights the importance of academic and clinical research in discovering new uses for existing drugs, suggesting that significant therapeutic advancements can occur outside traditional commercial frameworks. The findings advocate for increased support and recognition of these efforts in drug repurposing.

items.headline: Softness-driven cancer stem cells reprogrammed to defeat solid tumor resistance
items.preview: Research reveals how mechanical softness in tumors can create resistance to CAR-T cell therapies.
items.article:
A groundbreaking study has shown that cancer cells grown on soft matrices become less sensitive to CAR-T cell cytotoxicity. This research identifies a mechanism where sustained calcium signaling in soft-conditioned cells leads to a stem-like identity, enhancing their resistance to treatment.
Why this matters: By understanding how mechanical properties of the tumor microenvironment influence cancer cell behavior, researchers have developed a 'mechano-reprogrammer' that can convert resistant cells into targets for CAR-T therapy, potentially improving treatment outcomes for solid tumors.

items.headline: Engineering resilient gene drives for sustainable malaria control
items.preview: New research outlines a strategy to overcome resistance in gene drives targeting malaria mosquitoes.
items.article:
CRISPR-based gene drives have the potential to suppress malaria mosquito populations, but resistance can emerge. This study presents a pipeline to quantify the evolutionary space for resistance and develop multiplexed gene drives that target multiple sites to mitigate this issue.
Why this matters: By engineering resilient gene drives, researchers aim to enhance the effectiveness of malaria control strategies, ensuring that interventions can be sustained in natural populations despite the evolutionary pressures that may arise.
